Games]]}} {{MedalSilver | [[1972 Summer Olympics|1972 Munich]] | [[Basketball at the 1972 Summer Olympics|Team competition]] }} }} '''Robert Clyde Jones''' (born December 18, 1951) is an American former professional [[basketball]] player who played for the [[Denver Nuggets]] in the [[American Basketball Association]] (ABA) and the [[Philadelphia 76ers]] in the [[National Basketball Association]] (NBA). Nicknamed "'''the Secretary of Defense'''", Jones won an [[NBA Finals|NBA championship]] with the 76ers in [[1983 NBA Finals|1983]], was a four-time [[NBA All-Star]], a nine-time member of the [[NBA All-Defensive Team]], and was the [[NBA Sixth Man of the Year]] in [[1982–83 NBA season|1983]]. In 2019, Jones was elected to the [[Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame]].{{Cite news|url=https://chapelboro.com/sports/unc-sports/bobby-jones-elected-to-naismith-memorial-basketball-hall-of-fame|title=Bobby Jones elected to Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame|website=chapelboro.com|author=Avery Trendel|date=2018-04-07|access-date=2019-06-27}} ==Early life== Jones was born in [[Akron, Ohio]], but he and his family were constantly on the move.{{Cite web |last= |date=2008-04-07 |title=Living Against the Grain (Integrity - Chapter 5) {{!}} FCA Resources |url=https://fcaresources.com/devotional/living-against-grain-integrity-chapter-5 |access-date=2024-08-20 |website=fcaresources.com |language=en}} When he was in the sixth grade, they moved to [[Charlotte, North Carolina]], where they settled down. He grew up in a family that valued sports. His father J.R., a [[World War II]] veteran who had served in Japan, had played on the [[1946–47 Oklahoma Sooners men's basketball team|1947 Oklahoma Sooners]] national championship runner-up team and later on became a nationally ranked tennis player. His mother Hazel was a dominant high school athlete in basketball and tennis. Older brother Kirby was All-State in high school basketball and later a Sooner, who was also a state champion in tennis.{{Cite web |last=Rosen |first=Lauren |date=September 6, 2019 |title=Bobby Jones: A Hall of Fame Story |url=https://www.nba.com/sixers/bobby-jones-hall-fame-story |access-date=2024-08-19 |website=www.nba.com |language=en}} As a child, Jones often spent his days watching television, describing himself as a "[[couch potato]]".{{Cite web |last=Jones |first=Gordie |date=2019-04-09 |title=Winning Was Always The Point For Ex-76er Bobby Jones, Newly Minted Hall Of Famer |website=[[Forbes]] |url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/gordiejones/2019/04/09/winning-was-always-the-point-for-ex-76er-bobby-jones-newly-minted-hall-of-famer/#3a0019907d3c |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190409200034/https://www.forbes.com/sites/gordiejones/2019/04/09/winning-was-always-the-point-for-ex-76er-bobby-jones-newly-minted-hall-of-famer/#3a0019907d3c |archive-date=2019-04-09 |access-date=2024-08-20 }} J.R. then made him play on the church's league basketball team. When he was in sixth grade, his father built a basketball court. When his father was away working for [[Goodyear Tire and Rubber Company|Goodyear]], he would assign them drills to work on.{{Cite web |date=December 14, 2019 |title=GoHeels Exclusive: 'Great Memories' For Jones Upon Return |url=https://goheels.com/news/2019/12/14/mens-basketball-goheels-exclusive-great-memories |access-date=2024-08-20 |website=University of North Carolina Athletics |language=en}} One of those drills was shooting right-handed, despite being left-handed.{{Cite web |last=Fowler |first=Scott |date=April 1, 2019 |title=Is Charlotte's Bobby Jones finally about to make the Naismith Basketball Hall of Fame? |url=https://www.charlotteobserver.com/sports/spt-columns-blogs/scott-fowler/article228614349.html |access-date=August 19, 2024 |website=[[The Charlotte Observer]]}} He would do his drills during commercials.{{Cite web |last=Fitzpatrick |first=Frank |date=September 1, 2019 |title=At last, the Hall of Fame gets defensive and welcomes Sixers great Bobby Jones |url=https://www.inquirer.com/sixers/bobby-jones-sixers-76ers-hall-of-fame-induction-20190901.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191212193936/https://www.inquirer.com/sixers/bobby-jones-sixers-76ers-hall-of-fame-induction-20190901.html |archive-date=2019-12-12 |access-date=2024-08-21 |website=[[The Philadelphia Inquirer]]}} Eventually, he grew to enjoy the drills. As he got better at basketball, it became a way for him to socialize in high school and gain self-esteem.{{Cite web |last=Fowler |first=Scott |date=April 6, 2019 |title=Bobby Jones makes basketball Hall of Fame 33 years after retiring {{!}} Charlotte Observer |url=https://www.charlotteobserver.com/sports/spt-columns-blogs/scott-fowler/article228754944.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201118061943/https://www.charlotteobserver.com/sports/spt-columns-blogs/scott-fowler/article228754944.html |archive-date=2020-11-18 |access-date=2024-08-20 }}{{Cite news |last=Neff |first=Noel |date=September 7, 1983 |title=Ex-UNC star offers advice to persons with troubles |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=T-0eAAAAIBAJ&dq=bobby+jones+nba&pg=PA7 |access-date=August 21, 2024 |work=The Times-News |pages=13}} == High school career == Jones attended [[South Mecklenburg High School]] in [[Charlotte, North Carolina|Charlotte]], where played basketball and competed in track and field.{{Cite web |title=Bobby Jones Stats, Height, Weight, Position, Draft Status and more |url=https://www.basketball-reference.com/players/j/jonesbo01.html |access-date=2025-01-04 |website=Basketball-Reference.com |language=en}} His brother Kirby had also previously played for South Mecklenburg before playing for the Oklahoma Sooners.{{Cite book |last=Fowler |first=Scott |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=t4HFCs0WGQYC&dq=bobby%20jones%20%22kirby%22%20%22south%20mecklenburg%22&pg=PA91 |title=North Carolina Tar Heels: Where Have You Gone? |year=2005 |pages=91–94|publisher=Sports Publishing LLC |isbn=978-1-58261-942-2 }} Jones preferred track and field, because he could practice by himself on his own terms. He was a two-time state champion in the [[high jump]], finishing second his junior year to future North Carolina teammate and fellow NBA Hall of Famer [[Bob McAdoo]]. As a senior, Jones set a state record of 6 feet, 8 inches.{{Cite web |last=Wertz Jr. |first=Langston |date=October 6, 2021 |title=South Mecklenburg to honor athletic, academic greats Friday at Hall of Fame induction |url=https://www.charlotteobserver.com/sports/high-school/article254794962.html |access-date=August 20, 2024 |website=[[The Charlotte Observer]]}} Despite his track and field success, his father pushed him to pursue basketball. In basketball during his junior year, Jones earned Charlotte's Player of the Year Award and led South Mecklenburg into the state playoffs, where his squad lost to Greensboro Ben L. Smith that starred McAdoo. In his senior year, Jones led South Mecklenburg to the 1970 [[North Carolina High School Athletic Association|NCHSAA]] 4A state title and was also named MVP of the state championship game.[https://www.nchsaa.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/Mens-Basketball-Champs-and-MVPs.pdf Men’s Basketball Championship Results]. ''NCHSAA''. Retrieved October 29, 2025. Still, with all of his success in the sport, Jones did not think much about a future in it, but decided to pursue a basketball scholarship help pay for his education. He was recruited by the [[University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill|University of North Carolina]], [[Duke University]], and [[University of Florida|Florida]]. He also had interest in [[Davidson College]], as he regularly attended their games. His family also tried to convince him to play for [[University of Oklahoma|Oklahoma]], but it was too far for him. == College career == Jones chose North Carolina, as he connected with the coaching staff headed by [[Dean Smith]]{{Cite web |last=Jones |first=Gordie |date=September 6, 2019 |title=Ex-Sixer Bobby Jones, Far Tougher Than He Looks, Followed A Long, Hard Road To The Hall Of Fame |url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/gordiejones/2019/09/06/ex-sixer-bobby-jones-far-tougher-than-he-looks-followed-a-long-hard-road-to-the-hall-of-fame/ |access-date=2024-08-20 |website=Forbes |language=en}}, which included [[Bill Guthridge]] and [[John Lotz]]. NCAA eligibility rules at the time prohibited him from playing as a freshman,{{Cite web |last=DANIELS |first=ROB |date=2000-02-21 |title=JONES SORT OF FOLLOWING DAD'S FOOTSTEPS AT UNC\ AS BOBBY JONES' SON, ERIC JONES SAW BASKETBALL ROYALTY UP CLOSE AS A YOUNGSTER. |url=https://greensboro.com/jones-sort-of-following-dads-footsteps-at-unc-as-bobby-jones-son-eric-jones-saw/article_9dc97f0d-57f0-5913-b654-e9e94d5befdb.html |access-date=2024-08-20 |website=Greensboro News and Record |language=en}} allowing him to learn defensive skills from Smith and Guthridge. As a sophomore, Jones set an [[Atlantic Coast Conference]] single-season record 66.8% from the floor, and averaged 10.2 points and 6.3 rebounds a game while helping UNC reach the [[Final Four]]{{Cite web |last=Lawrence |first=Jake |date=2019-04-06 |title=UNC Basketball: Former UNC player Bobby Jones reportedly selected for Naismith Basketball Hall of Fame |url=https://www.tarheelblog.com/2019/4/6/18297993/former-unc-player-bobby-jones-reportedly-selected-for-nba-hall-of-fame-basketball-tar-heels |access-date=2024-08-21 |website=Tar Heel Blog |language=en}} (where they fell to the [[Florida State Seminoles men's basketball|Florida State Seminoles]]).{{Cite web |last=Mercer |first=Kevin |date=2019-04-08 |title=Hall of Fame inductee Bobby Jones says basketball has 'given me a platform to share my faith' |url=https://sportsspectrum.com/sport/basketball/2019/04/08/hall-of-fame-inductee-bobby-jones-says-basketball-has-given-me-a-platform-to-share-my-faith/ |access-date=2024-08-19 |website=Sports Spectrum |language=en-US}} After his time with the [[#National team career|U.S. national basketball team]], Jones started the gesture of pointing to teammates who passed him the ball to create a scoring opportunity, whether he made the shot or not. Coach Smith called the show of appreciation to his teammates "The Bobby Jones Rule".{{Cite news |last=Jones |first=Gordie |date=September 12, 2019 |title='A peaceful warrior': Distinguished by tenacity and grace, Bobby Jones caps off a Hall of Fame career |url=https://www.nytimes.com/athletic/1202427/2019/09/12/a-peaceful-warrior-distinguished-by-tenacity-and-grace-bobby-jones-caps-off-a-hall-of-fame-career/ |access-date=2024-08-20 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}} In his junior season, he averaged 15.5 points and 10.5 rebounds. The [[American Basketball Association|American Basketball Association (ABA)]]'s [[Carolina Cougars]] selected Jones after his junior season in the 1973 Special Circumstances Draft, but he wanted to finish his psychology degree and polish his game, so he returned to North Carolina for his senior year while the Cougars held on to his ABA rights. For his senior year, he was named co-captain of the team. He produced an [[NCAA Men's Basketball All-Americans|All-America]] campaign in 1973–74, averaging 16.1 points and 9.8 rebounds. He turned in memorable performances against Duke that season, including a clutch steal and game-winning layup against them in March. On UNC's "Senior Day", he contributed four points in the clutch as the team scored eight straight points to tie the game and eventually win in overtime 96–92.{{Cite web |title=Duke vs. North Carolina rivalry {{!}} Wins, highlights, memorable moments {{!}} NCAA.com |url=https://www.ncaa.com/news/basketball-men/article/2024-02-03/duke-vs-north-carolina-rivalry-wins-highlights-memorable-moments |access-date=2024-08-19 |website=www.ncaa.com |language=en}} He finished that game with 24 points.{{Cite web |title=The college careers of the 2019 Basketball Hall of Fame class {{!}} NCAA.com |url=https://www.ncaa.com/news/basketball-men/article/2019-09-05/college-careers-2019-basketball-hall-fame-class |access-date=2024-08-19 |website=www.ncaa.com |language=en}} Jones ended his career with averages of 13.7 points and 8.9 rebounds per game, while shooting 60.8% from the field; he graduated with his psychology degree.{{Cite web |date=2021-06-01 |title=TarHeelIllustrated - No. 25: Bobby Jones |url=https://northcarolina.rivals.com/news/no-25-bobby-jones |access-date=2024-08-20 |website=northcarolina.rivals.com}}{{Cite web |date=March 6, 2009 |title=Bobby Jones - The Gentleman of the NBA |url=https://www.nba.com/sixers/features/bobby_jones_090506.html |access-date=2024-08-20 |website=www.nba.com |language=en}} == Professional career == === Denver Nuggets (1974–1978) === ==== 1974–1976: ABA years ==== Jones was selected by the [[Houston Rockets]] with the fifth overall pick in the [[1974 NBA draft]].{{Cite web |last=Tomasson |first=Chris |date=2024-06-21 |title=McDonald's vs. '4-inch steaks': How the Nuggets beat Atlanta Hawks to David 'Skywalker' Thompson |url=https://denvergazette.com/sports/mcdonalds-vs-4-inch-steaks-how-the-nuggets-beat-atlanta-hawks-to-david-skywalker-thompson/article_2a8e89ac-2dde-11ef-9de0-0b629b6205f1.html |access-date=2024-08-20 |website=Denver Gazette |language=en}} Meanwhile, the Cougars franchise (then known as the [[Spirits of St. Louis]]), still held onto his ABA draft rights. Former Carolina Coach [[Larry Brown (basketball)|Larry Brown]] had moved on to the [[Denver Nuggets]], and he was determined to acquire him. The Nuggets traded for his rights with St. Louis in exchange for the rights to center [[Marvin Barnes]].{{Cite web |last=Watson |first=Phil |date=2016-08-05 |title=Denver Nuggets: 25 Best Players To Play For The Nuggets |url=https://hoopshabit.com/2016/08/05/denver-nuggets-25-best-players-to-play-for-the-nuggets/22/ |access-date=2024-08-20 |website=Hoops Habit |language=en-US}} Jones chose to join Denver, as he would have more playing time there. With Brown's coaching and Jones in the frontcourt, Denver went 65–19 in 1974–75, a 28-game improvement and franchise record.{{Cite news |last=Thompson II |first=Marcus |date=September 26, 2020 |title=Thompson: The Nuggets and a tradition of heartbreak at the hands of legends |url=https://www.nytimes.com/athletic/2094898/2020/09/26/thompson-the-nuggets-and-a-tradition-of-heartbreak-at-the-hands-of-legends/ |access-date=2024-08-20 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}} Jones shot .604 from the floor for an ABA record, scored 14.8 points per game, and won a spot on the ABA All-Rookie Team.{{Cite web |title=Remember the ABA: Bobby Jones |url=http://www.remembertheaba.com/TributeMaterial/BobbyJones.html |access-date=2024-08-21 |website=www.remembertheaba.com}} However, Denver lost to the [[Indiana Pacers]] in the Western Division Finals.{{Cite web |last=Moore |first=John |date=May 27, 2023 |title=Growing up with Nuggets in your blood {{!}} John Moore {{!}} Arts & Entertainment {{!}} denvergazette.com |url=https://denvergazette.com/arts-entertainment/growing-up-with-nuggets-in-your-blood-john-moore/article_517cbcd8-fc24-11ed-a6f2-23be563d0331.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230528063929/https://denvergazette.com/arts-entertainment/growing-up-with-nuggets-in-your-blood-john-moore/article_517cbcd8-fc24-11ed-a6f2-23be563d0331.html |archive-date=2023-05-28 |access-date=2024-08-20 }} In the [[1975–76 ABA season|1975–76 season]], the ABA's last, Jones averaged 15 points, nine rebounds, four assists, two steals, and two blocks, and once again topped the league in field-goal percentage. He also played in the [[1976 ABA All-Star Game]], where he scored 24 points with 10 rebounds, and was named to the All-ABA Second Team.{{Cite web |date=2024-07-01 |title=10 Greatest ABA Teams of All Time |url=https://www.legendssf.com/blogs/legends-blog/greatest-aba-teams-of-all-time?srsltid=AfmBOorZXkSK3yCYvOXnUDYpI9G_VRBLcARm-oaMXuOnX7cRoT4NFOO2 |access-date=2024-08-21 |website=Legends Clothing Co. |language=en}} The Nuggets, with stars [[David Thompson (basketball)|David Thompson]] and [[Dan Issel]], finished with a league-best 60–24 record, but fell to the [[New York Nets]] in the [[1976 ABA Finals|Finals]]. ==== 1976–1978; Transition to the NBA ==== The Nuggets transitioned to the NBA in 1976 as part of the [[ABA–NBA merger]]. In the [[1976–77 NBA season|1976–77 season]], Denver won the [[Midwest Division (NBA)|Midwest Division]].{{Cite web |last= |first= |date=2023-05-26 |title=The History of the Denver Nuggets |url=https://1stgensports.com/basketball/nba-basketball/1stgensports/the-history-of-the-denver-nuggets/ |access-date=2024-08-21 |website=1stgensports.com |language=en-US}} Jones averaged a career-high 15.1 points and 8.3 rebounds with a .570 field-goal percentage, and started in his first [[1977 NBA All-Star Game|NBA All-Star Game]] alongside Thompson and Issel.{{Cite web |last=Fromal |first=Adam |date=September 26, 2017 |title=Metrics 101: Greatest Power Forward Seasons in Modern NBA History |url=https://bleacherreport.com/articles/2734578-metrics-101-greatest-power-forward-seasons-in-modern-nba-history |access-date=2024-08-21 |website=[[Bleacher Report]] |language=en}}{{Cite news |date=February 11, 1977 |title=Jones Surprise All-Star Starter |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=5C4PAAAAIBAJ&dq=bobby+jones+nba&pg=PA25 |access-date=August 21, 2024 |work=[[The Victoria Advocate]]}} He also outpolled all other players in earning the first of eight straight selections to the [[NBA All-Defensive First Team]], as he had the best defensive rating in the league. They lost to the eventual champions the [[Portland Trail Blazers]] in the semis.{{Cite web |last=Walton |first=Michael |date=2019-09-10 |title=A nod to Bobby Jones, Hall of Famer and one of the greats in Denver Nuggets history |url=https://nugglove.com/2019/09/10/nod-bobby-jones-hall-famer-one-greats-denver-nuggets-history/ |access-date=2024-08-20 |website=Nugg Love |language=en-US}} The following season Jones averaged 14.5 points, elevated his field-goal percentage to a league-leading .578, and returned to the [[1978 NBA All-Star Game|All-Star Game]].{{Cite news |date=August 17, 1978 |title=Jones trade: McGinnis to Denver and Jones to 76ers |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=w7ssAAAAIBAJ&dq=bobby+jones+%2214.5+points%22&pg=PA42 |access-date=August 21, 2024 |work=Star-News |pages=2–D}}{{Cite web |title=1978 NBA All-Star recap |url=https://www.nba.com/news/history-all-star-recap-1978 |access-date=2024-08-21 |website=NBA.com |language=en}} Denver won their division once again.{{Cite book |last=Howell |first=Brian |title=Denver Nuggets |publisher=ABDO Publishing Company |year=2013 |pages=18}} However, due to the [[phenobarbital]] he was taking for his epilepsy, his performance dipped in the playoffs, and the Nuggets were eliminated in six games by the [[Seattle SuperSonics|Seattle Supersonics]] in the Western Conference finals.{{Cite web |last=Favakeh |first=Andrew |date=2021-06-18 |title=Bobby Jones, his epilepsy diagnosis, and me |url=https://www.libertyballers.com/2021/6/18/22540152/bobby-jones-his-epilepsy-diagnosis-and-me-philadelphia-76ers-nba |access-date=2024-08-19 |website=Liberty Ballers |language=en}} Denver management feared Jones would be limited by his health problems, as his epilepsy was getting worse throughout the season. This would be his final season in there. He finished his stint in Denver with averages of 14.8 points, 8.6 rebounds, 1.9 blocks and 2.0 steals per game. As of 2024 he was #7 on the team's all-time steals list, and #4 in all-time blocks.{{Cite web |title=Denver Nuggets Career Leaders |url=https://www.basketball-reference.com/teams/DEN/leaders_career.html |access-date=2024-08-20 |website=Basketball-Reference.com |language=en}} === Philadelphia 76ers (1978–1986) === ==== 1978–1979: First season ==== After the [[1977–78 NBA season|1977–78 campaign]] Jones was traded to the [[Philadelphia 76ers]] alongside [[Ralph Simpson]] for forward [[George McGinnis]] with both teams exchanging draft picks and both Jones and McGinnis waiving their no-trade clauses. The trade came with a clause that should Jones be disabled due to epilepsy, the 76ers would receive a draft pick. There he joined a team that was coached by another UNC alum, former forward and future NBA Hall of Famer [[Billy Cunningham]]. On March 7, 1979, he scored a career-high 33 points.{{Cite web |date=March 22, 2019 |title=The Hall of Fame Case for Bobby Jones {{!}} Offensive Opportunism |url=https://www.nba.com/sixers/history/hall-fame-case-bobby-jones-offensive-opportunism |access-date=2024-08-20 |website=www.nba.com |language=en}} That season, they won 47 games as he averaged 12.5 points, 6.5 rebounds, 2.5 assists, 1.3 steals, and 1.2 blocks per game, and led the league in field goal percentage. He was also selected to the First-Team All-Defense once again.{{Cite web |last=Fromal |first=Adam |date=March 30, 2015 |title=B/R NBA Legends 100: Ranking the Greatest Power Forwards of All Time |url=https://bleacherreport.com/articles/2215220-br-nba-legends-100-ranking-the-greatest-power-forwards-of-all-time |access-date=2024-08-21 |website=Bleacher Report |language=en}} ==== 1979–1982: Coming off the bench ==== Primarily a starter during his four seasons with the Nuggets, Jones made another transition after his first year with the Sixers. Coach Cunningham thought Jones would be best utilized as a sixth man, coming off the bench for the frontline [[Julius Erving]], [[Darryl Dawkins]], and [[Caldwell Jones]]. Cunningham was worried that the change would devastate Jones, but it took Jones about half a minute to agree to the coach's plan.{{Cite news |last=Goldaper |first=Sam |date=1981-02-01 |title=BOBBY JONES: A FIRST-CLASS SIXTH MAN |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1981/02/01/sports/bobby-jones-a-first-class-sixth-man.html |access-date=2024-08-21 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}} [[File:Bobby Jones NBA All-Defense.JPG|thumb|Certificate presented to Jones for [[NBA All-Defensive]] honors in 1981–82.]] Beginning with the [[1979–80 NBA season|1979–80 campaign]], Jones still averaged about 25 minutes. He also scored 14.4 points in his first season off the bench, his highest scoring average in his time with the Sixers. They won the Eastern conference championship but lost in the [[1980 NBA Finals ]] to the [[Los Angeles Lakers]] in six games that season. He returned to the NBA All-Star Game in 1981 as he was voted in by the coaches. Their season ended on a one-point loss to the [[Boston Celtics]] in the Eastern Conference finals. In [[1981–82 NBA season|1981–82]], Bobby Jones briefly returned to the starting lineup for that season, starting 73 games.{{Cite web |last1=Hudrick |first1=Paul |last2=Levick |first2=Noah |date=2020-05-27 |title=Ranking the 10 most important members of the 1982-83 Sixers |url=https://www.nbcsportsphiladelphia.com/nba/ranking-the-10-most-important-members-of-the-1982-83-sixers/317211/ |access-date=2024-08-21 |website=NBC Sports Philadelphia |language=en-US}} He was an All-Star again that season.{{Cite web |title=1982 NBA All-Star recap |url=https://www.nba.com/news/history-all-star-recap-1982 |access-date=2024-08-21 |website=NBA.com |language=en}} They avenged their loss to the Celtics the previous season in an Eastern Conference finals rematch, but lost once again to the Lakers in six games.{{Cite web |last=Prada |first=Mike |date=2020-04-14 |title=16 overachieving NBA teams who fell short of a title |url=https://www.sbnation.com/nba/2020/4/14/21216690/titleless-nba-teams-overachieved-fell-short-championship |access-date=2024-08-20 |website=SBNation.com |language=en}} ==== 1982–1983: Championship season ==== The arrival of star center [[Moses Malone]] from Houston for Caldwell Jones prior to the [[1982–83 Philadelphia 76ers season|1982–83 campaign]] was seen as a gamechanger for the Sixers' title hopes. In the regular season, they went on a 14-game win streak, and won 65 games. Bobby Jones finished the season third in the league in defensive box plus-minus. In the playoffs, the 76ers began with a sweep of the [[New York Knicks]], although each game was decided by fewer than 10 points. In game one of the conference finals, the [[Milwaukee Bucks]] led by 109–108 with one minute 36 seconds to go in overtime. [[Alton Lister]] of the Bucks tried to inbound the ball but Jones stole the pass and flipped the ball to [[Clint Richardson]]. Richardson scored on a dunk to send the 76ers ahead 110–109.{{Cite web |date=April 2, 2019 |title=The Hall of Fame Case for Bobby Jones {{!}} Clutch Contributions |url=https://www.nba.com/sixers/hall-fame-case-bobby-jones-clutch-contributions |access-date=2024-08-20 |website=www.nba.com |language=en}} A ''[[Philadelphia Inquirer]]'' article on Jones paraphrased the famous [[John Havlicek]] call by [[Johnny Most]] stating, "Bobby Jones stole the ball. It was grand larceny. Bobby Jones stole the ball and robbed the [[Milwaukee Bucks]] of a game, turning an almost-sure upset into a 111–109 overtime victory for the 76ers."[http://nl.newsbank.com/nl-search/we/Archives?p_product=PI&s_site=philly&p_multi=PI&p_theme=realcities&p_action=search&p_maxdocs=200&p_topdoc=1&p_text_direct-0=0EB2956A7A0459B5&p_field_direct-0=document_id&p_perpage=10&p_sort=YMD_date:D&s_trackval=GooglePM – Philadelphia Inquirer – May 9, 1983 – JONES STEALS ONE FOR THE SIXERS | Philly.com] In Game 2, he had a crucial block on [[Brian Winters]] that helped seal the win for the 76ers. After a Game 4 loss to Milwaukee, Philadelphia then rolled through the rest of the playoffs, eventually sweeping the Lakers in the [[1983 NBA Finals]]. After the season ended, Jones won the first-ever [[NBA Sixth Man of the Year Award]]. From the Eastern Conference finals to the [[1983 NBA Finals|NBA Finals]], he averaged 1.7 steals and 1.9 blocks.{{cite web |date=June 19, 2020 |title=The 10 best defenders in Sixers history {{!}} RSN – NBC Sports |url=https://www.nbcsports.com/philadelphia/76ers/sixers-history-best-defenders-bobby-jones-wilt-chamberlain-julius-erving-ben-simmons-joel-embiid |access-date=November 13, 2020 |publisher=[[NBC Sports]]}} ==== 1983–1986: Final seasons ==== The Sixers began a steady decline after that championship year, finishing second to [[Boston Celtics|Boston]] the next three seasons. While Jones continued to play steady defense, his offense began a gradual tail-off with reduced playing time and productivity. In the [[1985–86 NBA season|1985–86 season]] Jones only averaged 6.6 points per game despite returning to the starting lineup, but still shot a highly efficient .559 from the floor. That season, Philadelphia was eliminated by the Bucks in the playoffs.{{Cite web |last=Cialini |first=Joe |date=May 14, 1986 |title=Bobby Jones left basketball much the way he played... |url=https://www.upi.com/Archives/1986/05/14/Bobby-Jones-left-basketball-much-the-way-he-played/4085516427200/ |access-date=2024-08-20 |website=UPI |language=en}} Jones retired shortly afterward, on November 7, 1986, at age 34. The Sixers retired his uniform No. 24.{{Cite web |date=February 16, 2019 |title=Jones a Fitting Finalist for '19 HOF Class |url=https://www.nba.com/sixers/news/jones-fitting-finalist-19-hof-class |access-date=2024-08-21 |website=www.nba.com |language=en}} In his 12-year professional career, Jones was named to the [[NBA All-Defensive First Team]] eight times and the Second Team twice; earned the first-ever [[NBA Sixth Man Award]]; was on the ABA All-Rookie Team; was a four-time [[NBA All-Star Game|NBA All-Star]] and one time in the ABA; and won an [[NBA Championship]] with the [[Philadelphia 76ers]], in 1983.{{Cite web |date=July 18, 2011 |title=Exclusive Interview with Bobby Jones - 7/18/2011 |url=https://www.nba.com/sixers/features/exclusive_interview_with_bobby_2011_07_18.html |access-date=2024-08-20 |website=www.nba.com |language=en}}{{Cite web |title=NBA & ABA All-Rookie Teams |url=https://www.basketball-reference.com/awards/all_rookie.html |access-date=2024-08-21 |website=Basketball-Reference.com |language=en}} Over his career, he averaged 12.1 points and 6.1 rebounds, and his teams never missed the playoffs.{{cite web |author=Mike Singer |date=September 1, 2019 |title="Secretary of Defense" Bobby Jones reflects on colorful career as Hall of Fame enshrinement nears |url=https://www.denverpost.com/2019/09/01/bobby-jones-hall-of-fame-enshrinement-near/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201119195328/https://www.denverpost.com/2019/09/01/bobby-jones-hall-of-fame-enshrinement-near/ |archive-date=November 19, 2020 |access-date=November 13, 2020 |publisher=[[The Denver Post]]}} == National team career == In 1972, tryouts for the [[United States at the 1972 Summer Olympics|U.S. Olympic Team]] were about to be held. Jones was not invited to the trials at first, so he attended summer school. When [[Dean Smith]] heard that a couple of players were declining invitations as a form of protest, he got in touch with Jones.{{Cite web |last=Narducci |first=Marc |date=2012-08-29 |title=Defense put Bobby Jones on 1972 Olympic basketball team |url=https://www.inquirer.com/philly/sports/sixers/20120829_Defense_put_Bobby_Jones_on_1972_Olympic_basketball_team.html |access-date=2024-08-20 |website=[[The Philadelphia Inquirer]] |language=en}} After making sure Jones was healthy (as he was recovering from a seizure at the time) he invited him to the tryouts. Jones made the team, and quit summer school. He started all but one game due to a finger injury. He played only five minutes in the [[Soviet Union at the 1972 Summer Olympics|Soviet Union]]'s controversial win over the United States in the [[1972 Olympic men's basketball final|gold medal game]]. == Player profile == Jones was known as a versatile defensive player. Although listed as a power forward, he often guarded the other team's best small forward. In college, he could guard big men and guards. He was also known for being both active and athletic, which helped him deny the ball and box out for rebounds. A personal goal of his was to get at least 100 blocks and 100 steals every season, which he achieved six times. Jones is one of only seven players in both NBA and ABA history to total at least 1,300 blocks and 1,300 steals, with averages of 1.5 steals and 1.4 blocks.{{Cite web |date=March 13, 2019 |title=The Hall of Fame Case for Bobby Jones {{!}} Defensive Brilliance |url=https://www.nba.com/sixers/history/case-enshrinement-defense-became-jones-calling-card |access-date=2024-08-20 |website=www.nba.com |language=en}} In his NBA career, he made the top 20 in defensive rating six times. He made the ABA and [[NBA All-Defensive Team]] in almost every season he played, with his final NBA season being the only season he did not make any All-Defensive Team. He credits his time at North Carolina for his development on defense. Jones was not seen as a scorer, averaging 12.1 points per game in his career and scoring more than 30 points in a game only four times. When teams left him open however, he could make shots. Although he is not a three-point shooter (he shot 0-for-17 in his NBA career), he could make shots consistently from the elbow. At 6'9", he was also great at running fast breaks.{{Cite news |date=November 8, 1986 |title=Sixers Recognize Jones For Being Team Player |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=OrddAAAAIBAJ&dq=bobby+jones+aba+all-rookie+team&pg=PA18 |access-date=August 21, 2024 |work=[[The Victoria Advocate]] |pages=6B}} Those skills, along with being an ambidextrous finisher and being smart with his shot selection, helped give him a career field goal percentage of 56%. He never shot below 52% in any season of his career. His field goal percentage of 59.2 is the ABA's all-time record. He also rarely turned the ball over. Although he had the skills to be a starter, Jones often came off the bench.{{Cite web |date=2018-02-09 |title=Sixers Unveil Bobby Jones Statue - CBS Philadelphia |url=https://www.cbsnews.com/philadelphia/news/sixers-unveil-bobby-jones-statue/ |access-date=2024-08-19 |website=www.cbsnews.com |language=en-US}} This was good for him as it allowed him to scout the opposition and conserve energy for late-game situations. It also helped his physical condition, as he was taking medication for his epilepsy at the time. It was only in his first three seasons in the league that he averaged more than 30 minutes per game, while he averaged 25 minutes per game with the 76ers. Jones has been lauded for his selfless mentality and the intense effort he gave in games. "If I was going to ask a youngster to model after someone, I would pick Bobby Jones." said longtime 76ers teammate [[Julius Erving]], "He's a player who's totally selfless, who runs like a deer, jumps like a gazelle, plays with his head and heart each night, and then walks away from the court as if nothing happened."{{Cite web |last=Mickles |first=Stacey |date=2023-12-15 |title=The 10 best Philadelphia 76ers of all time |url=https://thecomeback.com/nba/philadelphia-76ers-best-greatest-irving-iverson-malone-embiid-chamberlain-barkley.html |access-date=2024-08-20 |website=The Comeback: Today's Top Sports Stories & Reactions |language=en-US}} Opponents called him "one of the toughest to play against". He was a part of 595 wins throughout his career from the ABA to the NBA, almost twice the number of games he lost. Jones was always honest and polite with referees. He would admit to referees if he was the one who sent the ball out of bounds or if he had fouled a player, even if it didn't help the team in the moment.{{Cite web |last=Jones |first=Gordie |date=September 7, 2019 |title=Hall Induction Is The Ultimate Honor For Ex-Sixer Bobby Jones, The Ultimate 'Anti-Scorer' |url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/gordiejones/2019/09/07/hall-induction-is-the-ultimate-honor-for-ex-sixer-bobby-jones-the-ultimate-anti-scorer/#14aaefb4e630 |access-date=2024-08-20 |website=Forbes |language=en}} [[Larry Brown (basketball)|Larry Brown]], Jones's coach with the [[Denver Nuggets]], remarked, "Watching Bobby Jones on the basketball court is like watching an honest man in a liars’ poker game."{{Cite web |date=April 6, 2019 |title=Former Nuggets ABA star Bobby Jones Selected for Naismith Basketball Hall of Fame Enshrinement |url=https://www.nba.com/nuggets/news/bobby-jones-selected-for-hall-of-fame-enshirement |access-date=2024-08-20 |website=www.nba.com |language=en}} As a result, referees would respect him and more calls would go their way.{{Cite web |last=Rhim |first=Kris |date=2019-09-06 |title=Legendary Sixer Bobby Jones on his love for Philly -- and its spaghetti |url=https://billypenn.com/2019/09/06/legendary-sixer-bobby-jones-on-his-love-for-philly-and-its-spaghetti/ |access-date=2024-08-20 |website=Billy Penn at WHYY |language=en-US}} Referee [[Joey Crawford]] said that Jones "was the most polite player" he ever dealt with.{{Cite web |last=Beck |first=Howard |author-link=Howard Beck |date=May 18, 2016 |title=Regrets, He's Had a Few: Joey Crawford Looks Back |url=https://thelab.bleacherreport.com/regrets-he-s-had-a-few-joey-crawford-looks-back/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160520045950/http://thelab.bleacherreport.com/regrets-he-s-had-a-few-joey-crawford-looks-back/ |url-status=dead |archive-date=May 20, 2016 |access-date=2024-08-20 |website=thelab.bleacherreport.com}} In his Naismith Hall of Fame speech, he gave credit to the referees. In his entire career, Jones was never called for a technical foul. |1.2 |11.9 |} == Endorsements == Jones endorsed [[Nike, Inc.|Nike]] throughout his career. In 1982, Jones was one of the first athletes to wear Nike's [[Air Force 1 (shoe)|Air Force 1]] sneakers.{{Cite web |title=Nike Basketball |url=https://www.sneakerfiles.com/nike/nike-basketball/ |access-date=2024-08-19 |website=www.sneakerfiles.com |language=en-US}} Nike also made a marketing campaign around him, which included a poster that dubbed him "The Secretary of Defense".{{Cite book |last=Croatto |first=Pete |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=syfODwAAQBAJ&dq=%22bobby%20jones%22%20nba%20%22nike%22%20%22secretary%22&pg=PA211 |title=From Hang Time to Prime Time: Business, Entertainment, and the Birth of the Modern-Day NBA |year=2020 |page=211|publisher=Simon and Schuster |isbn=978-1-9821-0397-2 }} == Post-retirement == In 1988, [[Billy Cunningham]], who had just helped establish the [[Miami Heat]], attempted to persuade Jones to play for Heat. After a physical and a scrimmage, he decided against returning. The [[Charlotte Hornets]] also tried to hire him as their general manager, but he turned them down. After retiring, Jones became a public speaker. He speaks at churches and schools, both local and international.{{Cite web |last=Hayes |first=Suzanne |date=March 16, 1991 |title=Ex-NBA star Bobby Jones to speak at awards dinner |url=https://www.tampabay.com/archive/1991/03/16/ex-nba-star-bobby-jones-to-speak-at-awards-dinner/ |access-date=2024-08-20 |website=Tampa Bay Times |language=en}}{{Cite web |last=Hurt |first=Cecil |date=November 9, 2003 |title=Former star Bobby Jones now lives low-key lifestyle |url=https://www.tuscaloosanews.com/story/news/2003/11/10/former-star-bobby-jones-now-lives-low-key-lifestyle/27851679007/ |access-date=2024-08-20 |website=The Tuscaloosa News |language=en-US}} He also stays in touch with the 76ers organization and is often invited to speak to the team. In 2003, Jones cofounded a [[Charlotte, North Carolina|Charlotte]], [[North Carolina]]–based religiously affiliated non-profit, 2xsalt, that supports underprivileged youth through sports, along with [[Bart Kofoed]] and former teammate [[David Thompson (basketball)|David Thompson]].{{Cite web |last= |date=2005-06-10 |title=Legends come to Lincolnton |url=https://www.lincolntimesnews.com/sports/legends-come-to-lincolnton/article_5baa71b7-326a-54c8-a96b-b47f34671d91.html |access-date=2024-08-19 |website=Lincoln Times News |language=en}} Jones has coached several school basketball teams in the Charlotte area including [[Charlotte Christian School]] for 12 years, where he won three state titles. He then became an assistant coach at Carmel Christian School.{{Cite web |last=Rayburn |first=Jim |date=December 16, 2003 |title=Ex-76ers star finds his niche on prep bench |url=https://www.deseret.com/2003/12/16/19801522/ex-76ers-star-finds-his-niche-on-prep-bench/ |access-date=2024-08-20 |website=Deseret News |language=en}} At Carmel Christian, he also coached their tennis team, held basketball clinics there, and was their summer camp coordinator. He also coached [[Myers Park High School]] and the South Charlotte Thunder.{{Cite web |title=History |url=https://www.southcharlottethunder.org/history |access-date=2024-08-20 |website=www.southcharlottethunder.org |language=en-US}} == Personal life == Jones is married and he and his wife have three children and seven grandchildren. They live in Charlotte, North Carolina. One of his sons, Eric, played for UNC's junior varsity team. Jones suffers occasional [[epileptic seizure]]s, which require medication. His first seizure occurred when he was a sophomore at UNC after an intramural volleyball game. At the time, he was misdiagnosed with [[pericarditis]], an inflammation of the heart sac. He experienced three more seizures from 1976 to 1978. In 1978, stricken by a seizure in his kitchen one day, Jones fell onto a [[butcher block]] and gashed open his head. The incident nearly led him to quit basketball. After he was traded to Philadelphia, he vowed to be more open about his diagnosis to break the stigma surrounding epilepsy. His perseverance earned him Philadelphia's Most Courageous Athlete Award in 1984, which he dedicated to his wife, Tess.{{Cite web |last=Juliano |first=Joe |date=January 24, 1984 |title=Bobby Jones doesn't dwell on the fact that an... - UPI Archives |url=https://www.upi.com/Archives/1984/01/24/Bobby-Jones-doesnt-dwell-on-the-fact-that-an/5017443768400/ |access-date=2024-08-20 |website=UPI |language=en}} He also suffered from a heart ailment, but after he was traded to Philadelphia, it never reoccurred again. Jones is a devout Christian. He grew up attending a Baptist church and devoted his life to Christ when he was in college. He said that the Bible affected how he played basketball, as it commanded followers to give their best in everything they did. When a computer-generated ranking sponsored by [[Seagram|Seagram Distillers]] rated Jones the NBA's "most consistent and productive player" in 1977, he donated the $10,000 prize to religious charities.{{Cite news |date=October 23, 1977 |title=Jones' Word Good |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=YQFKAAAAIBAJ&dq=nba+bobby+jones+%22seagram%22&pg=PA5 |access-date=August 20, 2024 |work=[[The Michigan Daily]] |pages=8}} [[Pat Williams (basketball)|Pat Williams]], the general manager of the 76ers at the time, credited him for helping establish pregame chapel services, which all NBA teams still do to this day.{{Cite web |last=Thomasos |first=Christine |date=2012-12-24 |title=NBA Legend Bobby Jones Recalls Glorifying God on Championship Path |url=https://www.christianpost.com/news/nba-legend-bobby-jones-recalls-glorifying-god-on-championship-path.html |access-date=2024-08-20 |website=www.christianpost.com |language=en}}{{Cite web |last=McGOWAN |first=CHLOE |date=2024-02-15 |title=NBA chaplains offer encouragement on and off the court |url=https://indianapolisrecorder.com/nba-chaplains-offer-encouragement-on-and-off-the-court/ |access-date=2024-08-20 |website=Indianapolis Recorder |language=en-US}} Throughout his ordeal with epilepsy, he credits his faith for helping him get through it. He is also active with Christian ministries such as the [[Fellowship of Christian Athletes]] (FCA) and [[Athletes in Action]].{{Cite web |last=Ford |first=Alan |date=December 13, 2016 |title=Ex-UNC, NBA star Jones share experiences |url=https://www.shelbystar.com/story/sports/pro/2016/12/14/ex-unc-nba-star-jones-share-experiences/24261678007/ |access-date=2024-08-20 |website=Shelby Star |language=en-US}} [[Cody Zeller]] credited Jones for helping him transition to the NBA as a spiritual mentor to him. [[Charles Barkley]] said of Jones, "If everyone in the world was like Bobby Jones, the world wouldn't have any problems."{{Cite web |last=King |first=J. D. |date=2023-04-25 |title=YouTube Gold: Bobby Jones |url=https://www.dukebasketballreport.com/2023/4/25/23697108/youtube-gold-bobby-jones-unc-dean-smith-nba-julius-erving-moses-malone-charles-barkley-andrew-tony |access-date=2024-08-20 |website=Duke Basketball Report |language=en}} == Legacy == The Sixers retired the No. 24 jersey in 1986. During his entire tenure with the Sixers, Jones' jersey always included the letter B with a period before his last name (B. JONES) above his number 24; he still wore it even after former teammate [[Caldwell Jones]] was traded for [[Moses Malone]] in 1982 and Caldwell's brother [[Charles Jones (basketball, born 1957)|Charles]] left after only one season with the Sixers ([[1983–84 NBA season|1983–84]]). However, during the 2008 season, as part of the Sixers' 25th anniversary of the 1983 champions, he was given a framed replica jersey that simply states his last name without the letter B, since he was the only Sixer named Jones to play on the 1983 team.{{citation needed|date=July 2024}} In 2018, a statue of him was unveiled at the Sixers' training complex. It shows him diving for a loose ball. In May 1989, Jones was inducted into North Carolina's Sports Hall of Fame.{{Cite news |date=March 17, 1999 |title=Former UNC star, NBA great to speak |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Wu0bAAAAIBAJ&dq=bobby+jones+aba+all-rookie+team&pg=PA4 |access-date=August 21, 2024 |work=[[The Dispatch]] |pages=7A}} On November 11, 2010, he was inducted into the Philadelphia Sports Hall of Fame.{{Cite web |title=Philadelphia Sports Hall of Fame Announces Seventh Inductee Class |url=http://www.phillyhall.org/content.asp?page=1&item=321¶m=2 |access-date=2024-08-21 |website=www.phillyhall.org}} In 2015, he was inducted into the FCA's Hall of Fame.{{Cite web |date= October 19, 2015 |title=FCA Announces Five Hall of Champions Inductees |url=https://www.fca.org/fca-in-action/blog-detail/2015/10/19/fca-announces-five-hall-of-champions-inductees |access-date=2024-08-20 |website=Default}} On April 6, 2019, he was elected to the [[Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame]]. He was inducted on September 6, 2019, with an introduction from Julius Erving and [[Charles Barkley]], who filled in for his coach Billy Cunningham and David Thompson. In 2021, he was inducted into South Mecklenburg's first-ever Hall of Fame. On January 28, 2020 [[Joel Embiid]] requested and was granted permission by Jones to wear his retired jersey number 24 for the Sixers, in honor of the late [[Kobe Bryant]].{{Cite web |date=2020-01-29 |title=Bobby Jones gave Joel Embiid one condition to wear retired number 24 for Kobe Bryant |url=https://www.yardbarker.com/nba/articles/bobby_jones_gave_joel_embiid_one_condition_to_wear_retired_number_24_for_kobe_bryant/s1_127_31164926 |access-date=2022-06-22 |website=Yardbarker |language=en}} In 2008, [[Athletes in Action]] named an award after him, the Bobby Jones Award, which recognizes an NBA player "who lives an exemplary life on the basketball court, in the home and in the community".{{Cite web |last=Phan |first=Katherine T. |date=2008-02-18 |title=Christian NBA Role Models Honored at All-Star Breakfast
